title: Jonah and the Weather
premise: Ines Quintana, once the most feared restaurant critic in Lisbon, lost his sense of taste three years ago and has survived by writing reviews of exquisite, evasive nothing. When his mother's house is sold, he finds a box of letters she wrote to his father—letters his father never received, because Ines's uncle intercepted them for forty years, including one that names a truth about Ines's paternity. As his mother's dementia advances and her memory dissolves, Ines must decide whether to deliver the final letter, confront the uncle who 'protected' them all, and finally write one honest sentence about food—and himself. He delivers it at his father's grave in the rain, then writes his last review: a single paragraph admitting he can no longer taste anything but remembers everything.
about_author: Oscar Galloway is the pen name of a former line cook who spent a decade writing menu copy before turning to fiction. He lives near the Atlantic coast, where he claims the weather does most of his editing.

chapters.title: The Palate of Ghosts
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. He reviews a celebrated tasting menu using pure invention, describing flavors he cannot perceive. At home he eats plain bread without pleasure. Emotional beat: the quiet shame of a man performing sensation he no longer feels.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Flashbacks to the stroke that took his taste; his editor praises his recent work as his 'most subtle.' His girlfriend Marta notices he never cooks anymore. Beat: the comfort and rot of a well-managed lie.

chapters.title: The House on Rua das Flores
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. His mother Leonor's house is sold; he returns to pack her things while she confuses him with his dead father. Beat: grief arriving sideways through misrecognition.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Moving the wardrobe, he finds a false back panel and a shoebox of unsent letters, all addressed to Tomás Quintana, postmarked across four decades. Beat: vertigo—the past was stored, not gone.

chapters.title: The First Letter
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, interleaved with Leonor's letter from 1979. She writes of a young wife's loneliness and a husband always at sea. Beat: Ines meets his mother as a stranger.

chapters.title: Uncle Amadeo
chapters.summary: Ines visits his uncle, now a placid widower tending tomatoes, and mentions the letters casually. Amadeo's fork pauses mid-air. Beat: the first crack in the family's polished surface.

chapters.title: What the Letters Say
chapters.summary: Ines reads chronologically at night: courtship, marriage, an accusation, a plea. One envelope is sealed and marked 'the last.' Beat: obsession replacing sleep; loyalty beginning to feel like complicity.

chapters.title: Marta's Question
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. She finds Ines asleep over the letters and asks what they are; he lies badly. Beat: the cost of inherited secrecy repeating itself in a new generation.

chapters.title: Leonor Remembers Everything
chapters.summary: A lucid afternoon: Leonor tells Ines about the letters as if he already knows, saying 'Amadeo said it was kinder not to send them.' Then she slips away again. Beat: the horror of a confession that won't hold still.

chapters.title: The Review That Fails
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Mid-review, his invented language collapses on the page; he submits something raw and true by accident. His editor calls, alarmed. Beat: the mask slipping publicly.

chapters.title: Amadeo's Version
chapters.summary: Amadeo's POV. He explains: Tomás was violent, the letters were full of Leonor leaving, and intercepting them kept a family intact—or so he told himself for forty years. Beat: sympathy and fury entangled.

chapters.title: The Sealed Envelope
chapters.summary: Ines steams open the last letter against every instinct. Inside: a single page naming Ines's biological father—not Tomás. Beat: identity detonated in one sentence.

chapters.title: Weather Report
chapters.summary: Ines walks the city in a storm, unable to go home or to Amadeo's. A chance meal at a cheap tasca where he tastes nothing, weeps anyway. Beat: breakdown as clearing weather.

chapters.title: What Marta Knew
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. She reveals she found a hospital record months ago suggesting the truth and stayed silent to protect him. Beat: mirror held up—invisibility chosen by love is still a lie.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Tomato Rows
chapters.summary: Ines demands why Amadeo hid even this. Amadeo admits the interception wasn't only protection—it was jealousy, a brother's theft dressed as mercy. Beat: the moral center gives way; no clean villain.

chapters.title: Leonor's Last Clear Day
chapters.summary: Ines brings the letters to Leonor. For ten minutes she is fully present, reads her own words aloud, and says, 'Send them. I was braver than you let me be.' Beat: absolution that is also an indictment.

chapters.title: The Undelivered Address
chapters.summary: Ines learns Tomás didn't die at sea as told—he lived twenty years in Porto, died alone. The letters could have reached a living man. Beat: grief compounded by stolen time.

chapters.title: Porto in the Rain
chapters.summary: Ines travels to the cemetery, letters in his coat. Standing at the unmarked plot, he cannot read them aloud; a stranger assumes he's mourning his father, and he lets the assumption stand—then corrects it. Beat: choosing truth in miniature before the grand gesture.

chapters.title: Delivered
chapters.summary: Climax. Ines buries the letters at the grave, reads the last one to the rain, and calls Amadeo to say it's done. Amadeo says nothing for a long time, then: 'Thank you. I couldn't.' Beat: release without forgiveness.

chapters.title: One Honest Sentence
chapters.summary: Ines writes his final review: no dish, no adjectives—just the admission that taste left him and memory remained, and that both were worth having. He resigns. Beat: professional death as personal birth.

chapters.title: Salt
chapters.summary: Epilogue-adjacent. Months later, cooking for Marta in a borrowed kitchen, Ines salts soup and tastes—faintly, maybe—something. Or imagines it. He decides it doesn't matter. Beat: grace ambiguous and accepted.

chapters.title: Jonah and the Weather
chapters.summary: Closing chapter. Ines visits Leonor, who no longer knows him but offers him bread, and he eats it like communion. Walking home under a clearing sky, he begins a new notebook titled with the book's name. Beat: peace earned, story continuing beyond the last page.
